claims.text: An ultra-high-cooling-rate solidification followed immediately by a sub-Tg isothermal hold will improve both glass-forming ability and amorphous-state thermal stability relative to single-stage rapid quenching.
Conventional rapid solidification can produce an amorphous phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy.
The baseline amorphous alloy has moderate glass-forming ability and thermal stability.
Very rapid cooling can produce an amorphous phase in a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy.
A cooling rate significantly higher than conventional rates kinetically arrests nucleation.
A hold near Tg - 5 K can permit structural relaxation while preserving the amorphous structure.
The two-stage treatment reduces residual internal stresses in the amorphous matrix.
The two-stage treatment decreases the number of active nucleation sites in the amorphous matrix.
Ultra-high-rate cooling minimizes nucleus formation by sharply reducing atomic mobility.
A sub-Tg hold produces a lower-energy, structurally relaxed glass without initiating crystallization.
The proposed processing route decouples structural relaxation and stress relief from crystallization kinetics.
The two-stage process will increase the critical casting diameter relative to single-stage quenching.
The two-stage process will increase the DSC crystallization-onset temperature relative to single-stage quenching.
The two-stage process will reduce residual internal stress relative to single-stage quenching.
The intervention may fail if the cooling rate is inadequate or the sub-Tg hold temperature or duration is not optimally controlled.
Alloys with substantially different nucleation kinetics or intrinsic phase stability may not benefit from the intervention.
The optimal sub-Tg temperature, hold duration, and magnitude of improvement depend on alloy composition and remain to be determined.
